questions.stem: In a secret code FLIGHT is written as VBYWXJ. How would the word WORLD be written?
questions.hint: Write the alphabet on one line and the code letters on the line below. Find how many places F moves to become V, then check that L moves the same number of places to become B.

steps.explain: A code like this moves every letter the same number of places along the alphabet. Compare the first letter of FLIGHT with the first letter of its code to find the rule.
steps.work: \(F \rightarrow V\) F is the 6th letter and V is the 22nd letter, so F has moved \(22-6=16\) places forward.

steps.explain: Check the rule with a second letter. If the rule is right, L must become B.
steps.work:
\(L\) is the 12th letter: \(12+16=28\). The alphabet only has 26 letters, so go past Z and start again at A: \(28-26=2\), the 2nd letter, which is B. ✓

The rule is: move every letter 16 places forward (wrapping round from Z back to A). The six pairs F→V, L→B, I→Y, G→W, H→X, T→J all follow it.

steps.explain: Put the code letters together in the same order as WORLD and find the matching option.
steps.work: WORLD \(\rightarrow\) M E H B T = MEHBT. This is option B.

steps.explain: Quick check of the other options: each one has a letter that does not match the rule.
steps.work: A (NEHBT) starts with N, but W gives M. C (MEGBS) has G in 3rd place, but R gives H. D (MFHBR) has F in 2nd place, but O gives E.

keyPoints.note: Compare each plain letter with its code letter. The same rule is used for every letter.
Apply the rule you found to each letter of WORLD, one letter at a time.

questions.stem:
When these words are put together in the correct order they will make a sentence. Which is the last word in the correct sentence?

gain then 305E dial to the in use intercom order entry
questions.hint: Look for word pairs that belong together, such as “in order to” and “gain entry”. Build the whole sentence from the front, then see which word is left for the end.

steps.explain: Find the groups of words that naturally go together.
steps.work: “in order to” is a common phrase. “gain entry” goes together. “dial 305E” goes together (305E is what you dial).

steps.explain: Join the groups into a sentence, starting with the phrase that sounds like a beginning.
steps.work: In order to gain entry, dial 305E then use the intercom.

steps.explain: Check that every word has been used exactly once.
steps.work: in, order, to, gain, entry, dial, 305E, then, use, the, intercom — 11 words, the same 11 words as in the question. ✓

steps.explain: Read off the last word of the sentence.
steps.work: The last word is “intercom”. The answer is D. (“speak” is not in the list at all.)

keyPoints.note: Build the whole sentence first, then read its last word.
The finished sentence must make sense and use every word once.

questions.stem: EAR is to LISTEN as TONGUE is to ?
questions.hint: Turn the first pair into a sentence: “You use your ear to …”. Then use the same sentence pattern with TONGUE.

steps.explain: Find the relationship in the first pair of words.
steps.work: You use your EAR to LISTEN. (body part → the action it does)

steps.explain: Use the same relationship for TONGUE. What do you do with your tongue?
steps.work: You use your TONGUE to TASTE.

steps.explain: Check each option against the relationship (body part → action).
steps.work: taste ✓ an action done with the tongue. flavour — this is what you taste, not an action. lips — another body part, not an action. words — what you say, not an action.

steps.explain: The pair that matches EAR : LISTEN is TONGUE : TASTE.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Work out how these two words are linked before looking at the options.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: ‘The school principal will decide which pupils will be given a prize’. What is the meaning of DECIDE in the previous sentence?
questions.hint: Put each option into the sentence in place of DECIDE and ask: does the sentence still mean the same thing?

steps.explain: Think about what the principal does in the sentence.
steps.work: The principal chooses which pupils get a prize — a final choice is made.

steps.explain: Try each option in place of “decide”.
steps.work:
recommend: “will recommend which pupils…” only suggests, nobody has chosen yet.

define: means “explain what a word means” — it does not fit.

consider: “will consider which pupils…” means think about it, but not the final choice.

determine: “will determine which pupils…” means settle it for certain. ✓

steps.explain: Both DECIDE and DETERMINE mean to settle something finally.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Here “decide” means to make the final choice, not just to think or suggest.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage and then answer the questions below.

In January this year, the Mars Polar Lander made a perfect launch to search for water on the planet Mars. Polar Lander will team up with a sister ship, the Mars Climate Orbiter, launched a month ago. The Orbiter will arrive in September this year to survey weather patterns on the red planet.

The Polar Lander is on a 756 million kilometre mission that hopes to find proof of frozen water near the planet’s south pole. The discovery of water traces could help scientists find out whether some form of life existed on Mars. Geologists think that water once flowed on Mars.

Polar Lander will fire microprobes into the surface of Mars at a speed of 650 km/h. These will rest about 1 metre below the surface and will be about 100 km from where the Polar Lander touches down. Once on the ground next December, the Polar Lander will also dig into the surface and obtain soil samples, analyse gases and look for traces of water vapour. The spacecraft will send back video and weather data for about 60–90 days before its instruments freeze in the Martian autumn where a year lasts 687 days.

Source: Adapted from Roman Chester, Courier Mail, 5 January 1999

parts.stem: What would be a key title for this passage?
options: NASA on its way back to Mars
Scientists search for water on surface of red planet
Mars Orbiter makes a perfect launch
parts.hint: A key title tells the main idea of the whole passage in a few words. Ask yourself: what is the passage mostly about from start to finish?

steps.explain: A title must fit the WHOLE passage, not just one small detail. Say in your own words what the passage is about.
steps.work: The Mars Polar Lander is travelling to Mars to search for water — it hopes to find proof of frozen water near the south pole.

steps.explain: Test each title against the passage.
steps.work:
A “NASA on its way back to Mars” — nothing in the passage says NASA is going back.

C “NASA mission to study climate” — only the Orbiter surveys weather; the main mission is the search for water.

D “Mars Orbiter makes a perfect launch” — it was the Polar Lander that made the perfect launch, and that is only one detail.

B “Scientists search for water on surface of red planet” — matches the passage from beginning to end. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the title that covers the main idea.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A key title states the main idea of the whole passage, not one small detail.

parts.stem: What does the article show?
options: The mission hopes to find proof of water on the red planet
The search should attract lots of attention later this year
This is a US mission that lifted off from Cape Canaveral
Polar Lander made a perfect launch
parts.hint: The question asks what the article is mainly telling us. Choose the statement that is directly stated and sums up the purpose of the mission.

steps.explain: Ask what the article is mainly trying to tell the reader — its main message.
steps.work: The second paragraph says the mission hopes to find proof of frozen water near the planet’s south pole.

steps.explain: Check each option against the passage.
steps.work:
B “attract lots of attention” — the passage never says this.

C “lifted off from Cape Canaveral” — the passage never names the launch site.

D “made a perfect launch” — this is stated, but it is only a small detail in the first sentence, not what the article shows.

A “hopes to find proof of water on the red planet” — stated, and it is the purpose of the whole mission. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the statement that gives the main message.
steps.work: The answer is A.

parts.stem: What main point does the article indicate?
options: Maps of the weather patterns will show whether microbial life exists
The microprobes will provide accurate images of the surface
Traces of water vapour will show whether water once flowed on Mars
Mars Orbiter and Polar Lander will land three months apart
parts.hint: The main point is the big idea behind the mission. Which option links the search for water traces to what scientists want to find out?

steps.explain: The main point is the big idea the writer wants us to take away. Look for the reason why scientists are doing the mission.
steps.work: “The discovery of water traces could help scientists find out whether some form of life existed on Mars. Geologists think that water once flowed on Mars.”

steps.explain: Check each option against the passage.
steps.work:
A — the Orbiter surveys weather patterns, but nothing links weather maps to life.

B — the microprobes are fired into the surface, but “accurate images” are not mentioned.

D — the Orbiter arrives in September and the Lander lands in December, but this is a small detail, not the main point.

C — the Lander will “look for traces of water vapour”, which would show that water once flowed. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the option that matches the main idea.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The main point is the biggest idea in the passage, not a small fact.

meta.source: Excel Practice Opportunity Class Tests · Year 4

parts.stem:
Here are three facts from the passage. They are numbered 1, 2 and 3. Read them then put them in the correct order to show that it is possible that life existed on Mars.

1 — It is possible that life existed on Mars because water vapour is necessary for life.
2 — If the soil near the South Pole is analysed and traces of water vapour are found
3 — Then water once flowed on Mars
parts.hint: Look at the first words of each fact (“If”, “Then”, “It is possible … because”). Which one sets up a condition, which one follows from it, and which one is the final conclusion?

steps.explain: Look at the linking words that start each fact.
steps.work:
1 — “It is possible that life existed… because…” is a conclusion.

2 — “If the soil… is analysed and traces… are found” sets up a condition.

3 — “Then water once flowed on Mars” must follow an “If”.

steps.explain: Build the chain of reasoning: condition → result → conclusion.
steps.work:
2 → 3 → 1

If traces of water vapour are found (2), then water once flowed on Mars (3), so it is possible that life existed there, because water is necessary for life (1).

steps.explain: Check the options: fact 3 starts with “Then”, so it cannot come first, which removes options A and B. Fact 1 is the conclusion, so it cannot come first either, which removes option C.
steps.work: The order 2 3 1 is option D.

keyPoints.note: A good order moves from the condition (“If…”) to the result (“Then…”) to the conclusion.

keyPoints.text: it is possible that life existed on Mars
keyPoints.note: This is the conclusion that the three facts must lead to.

questions.stem: NOON is to SUN as MIDNIGHT is to ?
questions.hint: Think about what you can see high in the sky at NOON. Then think about what you can see in the sky at MIDNIGHT.

steps.explain: Find the link in the first pair of words.
steps.work:
NOON is the middle of the day, and the SUN is what we see high in the sky at that time.

(time of day → what you see in the sky)

steps.explain: Use the same link for MIDNIGHT. It is the middle of the night, so what do we see in the sky?
steps.work: At midnight it is dark and we see the STARS.

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
SUNSET, TWILIGHT and EVENING are all times of day, not things you can see in the sky. SUN is a thing in the sky, so we need a thing, not a time.

STARS is a thing you can see at midnight. ✓

steps.explain: The pair that matches NOON : SUN is MIDNIGHT : STARS.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: First find the link: what do you see in the sky at noon?
Midnight is the middle of the night. Use the same link.

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

THE ROAD TO MULLAWALLA

In the back of the blue car the boy sat among the piled luggage. He heard the aircraft droning above and leant over some of the bags to look out the far window. Sunlight flashed on the small plane, startling silver against the blue. Now it was almost overhead.

‘Why didn’t we come by plane, Dad?’ he grumbled. But of course he knew the answer. The car had to be driven up — if only to carry all the personal stuff on the roof-rack and in the boot stacked beside him. The furniture had been sent on ahead. For the past hour his mother had been worrying aloud that it might not be waiting in the new house for them as promised. She had just finished her turn at driving and was sitting back, eyes closed. Frank knew she didn’t want to live out here any more than he did.

There had been nightly arguments between his parents for the last few weeks. Well, who would want to leave the beaut Gold Coast? He’d always lived there. It had amusement arcades and Seaworld and Dreamworld — and the beaches of course. The surf carnivals were OK too, and there was TV. There was only one TV channel where they were going. It was rotten luck all right, his father being transferred by the bank. ‘Promoted’ to manager in this horrible little town with the silly name, Mullawalla.

Source: Elsie Young, The Secret of Yesterday Hills, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990, p.4

parts.stem: Which is the most important fact in this passage?
options: Frank did not want to leave the Gold Coast
Frank’s family was travelling with all their belongings
Frank was bored sitting in the back seat
parts.hint: The most important fact is the one the whole passage is built around. Ask: why is Frank unhappy, and what is the story really about?

steps.explain: The most important fact is the main idea — the one that explains the rest of the passage, not a small detail.
steps.work: Look at what Frank thinks and feels in the passage.

steps.explain: Find the evidence that shows how Frank feels about the move.
steps.work:
“Frank knew she didn’t want to live out here any more than he did.” — he did not want to live out here

“Well, who would want to leave the beaut Gold Coast? He’d always lived there.”

“It was rotten luck all right…”

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
B — the car carries their belongings, but this is only a small detail.

C — the mother has her eyes closed, but nobody says Frank is tired.

D — nothing says Frank is bored in the back seat.

A — the whole passage is about Frank not wanting to leave the Gold Coast. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the fact that matches the main idea.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Pick the fact the whole passage is about, not a small detail.

meta.source: Excel Practice Opportunity Class Tests · Year 4

parts.stem: What can you conclude about the move to Mullawalla?
options: The journey was an adventure for the whole family
His father and mother did not agree to move
It was his father’s idea to move to Mullawalla
parts.hint: To conclude means to work out something from clues. Look for clues about how Frank’s mother and father feel about moving.

steps.explain: A conclusion is something you work out from the clues in the passage.
steps.work: Look for clues about the parents.

steps.explain: Find the clues.
steps.work:
“There had been nightly arguments between his parents for the last few weeks.”

“Frank knew she didn’t want to live out here any more than he did.” (his mother)

“…his father being transferred by the bank.”

steps.explain: Put the clues together and check each option.
steps.work:
The parents argued every night, and the mother did not want to move, so the parents did not agree. ✓ (B)

A — the family is not enjoying the trip.

C — they are moving there, not visiting.

D — it was the bank that transferred the father, not his own idea.

steps.explain: Choose the conclusion supported by the clues.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A conclusion is worked out from clues in the passage. It is not stated directly.

meta.source: Excel Practice Opportunity Class Tests · Year 4

parts.stem: What does this phrase — ‘in this horrible little town with the silly name, Mullawalla’ tell us about Frank?
options: He had lived in Mullawalla before and hated it
He only wanted to live in a city
He was already biased about Mullawalla
He did not like the name Mullawalla
parts.hint: Frank is still on the road. Has he seen Mullawalla yet? What does it mean to judge a place before you know it?

steps.explain: Notice where Frank is when he thinks this.
steps.work: He is in the car on the way to the new town. He has not arrived, so he has not seen Mullawalla yet.

steps.explain: Look at the words Frank uses to describe the town.
steps.work:
“…in this horrible little town with the silly name, Mullawalla.”

He already thinks the town is horrible, even though he has never been there.

steps.explain: Biased means having an opinion before you know the facts. Check the options.
steps.work:
A — he had always lived on the Gold Coast, not in Mullawalla.

B — nothing says he only wanted a city.

D — the name is only part of what he dislikes: he also calls the town “horrible” and “little”.

C — he judges Mullawalla before seeing it. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the option that fits.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The phrase shows how Frank feels. Think about what he knows about the town so far.
The name is only part of the phrase — look at all the words Frank uses.

parts.stem: What does the word ‘transferred’ mean in this passage?
parts.hint: Read the sentence around the word. Where is the father going because of the bank? Which option means “sent to a new place to work”?

steps.explain: Read the whole sentence that contains the word.
steps.work: “…his father being transferred by the bank. ‘Promoted’ to manager in this horrible little town…”

steps.explain: Work out what happened to the father.
steps.work: He is being sent by the bank to work in a different town, as manager. (The family has to move because of his job.)

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
employed — he already works for the bank.

retrenched — means losing a job, but he was promoted.

driven — they are driving to the town, but the bank did not drive him.

assigned — given a new job in a new place. ✓

steps.explain: “Transferred” and “assigned” both mean given a new place to work.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Read the full sentence. The bank is sending the father to a new job in a new town.

parts.stem: How many things would Frank miss from the Gold Coast?
parts.hint: Read the third paragraph and list each thing Frank likes about the Gold Coast. Tick them off one by one as you count.

steps.explain: Find the sentences where Frank lists what he likes about the Gold Coast.
steps.work: “It had amusement arcades and Seaworld and Dreamworld — and the beaches of course. The surf carnivals were OK too, and there was TV. There was only one TV channel where they were going.”

steps.explain: Count each different thing.
steps.work:
1. amusement arcades

2. Seaworld

3. Dreamworld

4. the beaches

5. the surf carnivals

6. TV (more than one channel)

questions.stem: Which phrase has most nearly the same meaning as FOSSIL?
options: ancient preserved remains in the earth’s crust
mysterious bones and shells in the soil
questions.hint: A fossil is something very old. Think about what a fossil actually is, not where you might see one or who finds one.

steps.explain: Decide what a fossil is in your own words.
steps.work: A fossil is the preserved remains (or print) of a plant or animal that lived a very long time ago, found in rock.

steps.explain: Check each phrase.
steps.work:
B — “mysterious” is not part of the meaning, and fossils are found in rock, not just soil.

C — this describes scientists at work, not the fossil itself.

D — this is where you may see fossils, not what a fossil is.

A — “ancient preserved remains in the earth’s crust” is what a fossil is. ✓

steps.explain: Choose the phrase that is the definition.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Choose the phrase that explains what a fossil is, not where it is found or who finds it.

questions.stem:
Read the lines of this poem ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’ by Alfred, Lord Tennyson. Which words should fill the blank spaces ________ in the poem?

Half a league, half a league,
Half a league ________,
All in the valley of Death
Rode the six hundred.
‘Forward, the Light Brigade!
Charge for the guns!’ he said:
Into the ________ of Death
Rode the six hundred.
questions.hint: Read the poem aloud. The riders are told “Forward!” — which word fits that direction? And look back at line 3 to find a place that is repeated.

steps.explain: Look at the first blank: “Half a league ________,”. The riders are told “Forward, the Light Brigade!”
steps.work: They are going forward, so the word must be onward, not backward.

steps.explain: Look at the second blank: “Into the ________ of Death”. The poem repeats words, and line 3 says something very similar.
steps.work:
“All in the valley of Death” … “Into the ________ of Death”

The same place is named again: valley.

steps.explain: Check the other words.
steps.work:
backward — the opposite of forward, so it does not fit.

gully — a small valley, but the poem uses the word “valley”.

galley — a ship’s kitchen, which does not fit a charge into battle.

steps.explain: The two words are onward and valley.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: Which words should fill the blank spaces
keyPoints.note: Use clues in the poem: the direction the riders are told to go, and the place named earlier.

questions.stem: LOW is to HIGH as SHALLOW is to ?
questions.hint: Check how the first two words are related. Are they the same, or opposites? Then find the opposite of SHALLOW.

steps.explain: Find the link between LOW and HIGH.
steps.work: LOW and HIGH are opposites (antonyms).

steps.explain: Find the opposite of SHALLOW.
steps.work: SHALLOW describes water that is not far down. The opposite is DEEP.

steps.explain: Check the options.
steps.work:
more — not a depth word. depth — a noun (the measurement), but LOW and HIGH are describing words, so we need a describing word too. fathom — a unit of depth, not an opposite.

deep ✓

steps.explain: LOW : HIGH matches SHALLOW : DEEP.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: LOW and HIGH are opposites. Use the same link for SHALLOW.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

TIME CAPSULE

Elizabeth was a Woodhouse too, though not at all like Anne and James, who were both blue-eyed and fair. She was exciting and different, somehow. Anne and James loved having her over for the summer holidays.

If there was one thing Cousin Elizabeth was good at, it was telling the most amazing stories about the past; and sometimes, about the future.

‘Come on, you pair of lazy layabouts!’ she laughed as Anne and James came into the kitchen.

‘Breakfast is ready, so hurry up. I’m taking you both out for a long walk today.’

‘Where are we going?’ James asked, his mouth full of porridge.

‘Somewhere special’, said Cousin Elizabeth.

‘Are we taking lunch?’ Anne was very practical.

‘Yes. Your mother has a cold pie for us in the meatsafe.’

Anne and James gulped their porridge, washed it down with glasses of milk, then scraped the dishes clean in the tin tub.

‘It’s going to be hot. We had better take hats,’ said Anne, jamming on her flowered bonnet.

All strange feelings were forgotten as the three of them stepped out into the bright sunlight and headed for the bush track.

‘Be careful, children’, Mrs Woodhouse called. ‘Don’t wander away and get lost.’

‘I’ll keep an eye on these two rascals’, Cousin Elizabeth said, straightening James’ shirt.

The three of them linked arms, chattering as they walked along the dusty dirt track.

Source: Rachael Collinson, Time Capsule, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

parts.stem: When and where does this story probably take place?
options: summer time recently and in the country
summer time some time ago and in the country
spring time some time ago and in the country
summer time some time ago and in the city
parts.hint: There are three clues to find: the season, how long ago, and the place. Look for words like “hot”, “meatsafe”, “tin tub” and “bush track”.

steps.explain: Find the clues for the season (when).
steps.work: “…summer holidays” and “It’s going to be hot” and “the bright sunlight” → summer.

steps.explain: Find the clues for how long ago.
steps.work: “a cold pie… in the meatsafe”, “the dishes clean in the tin tub” and a “flowered bonnet” are old-fashioned things → some time ago, not recently.

steps.explain: Find the clues for the place.
steps.work: “…headed for the bush track” and “the dusty dirt track” → in the country, not in the city.

steps.explain: Put the three answers together.
steps.work: summer + some time ago + in the country. The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Use clues in the story. “Probably” means you work it out, it is not stated.

parts.stem: Whom would you say was a ‘lazy layabout’?
parts.hint: Find who says “lazy layabouts” and who she is talking to. Then see which option is one of those people.

steps.explain: Find the words in the passage.
steps.work: “Come on, you pair of lazy layabouts!” she laughed as Anne and James came into the kitchen.”

steps.explain: Elizabeth is talking to Anne and James, who have just come into the kitchen.
steps.work: So the “lazy layabouts” are Anne and James. Only one of these two is an option: James.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Mrs Woodhouse is the mother who calls out later. Mr Woodhouse is not in the story. Elizabeth is the one speaking — she is not lazy, she is cooking breakfast and taking them for a walk.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Look for the words in the passage and see who they are said to.

parts.stem: What talent did Elizabeth have?
parts.hint: A talent is something a person is good at. Find the sentence that says what Elizabeth was good at.

steps.explain: A talent is something you are especially good at. Find where the passage says what Elizabeth was good at.
steps.work: “If there was one thing Cousin Elizabeth was good at, it was telling the most amazing stories about the past; and sometimes, about the future.”

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — going for long walks is something she does, not something she is good at.

B — “exciting and different” describes her, it is not a talent.

D — minding Anne and James is a job she does in the story.

steps.explain: Her talent was telling amazing stories.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: A talent is something a person is especially good at.

steps.explain: Go through the story and list each different person.

2. Anne

3. James

4. Mrs Woodhouse (“Your mother has a cold pie for us…” — their mother)

parts.stem: How do we know that the children were going to be away for some hours?
options: Mr Woodhouse told them not to wander away
parts.hint: What do people take with them when they will be away from home for a long time? Look for a clue in the dialogue.

steps.explain: Find what they say before they leave.
steps.work:
“Are we taking lunch?” Anne was very practical.

“Yes. Your mother has a cold pie for us in the meatsafe.”

steps.explain: Think about why they need lunch.
steps.work: You only take lunch when you will be away from home at lunchtime — for several hours.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — it being holiday time does not say how long they will be away.

B — Mr Woodhouse is not in the story (it was Mrs Woodhouse who spoke).

C — a bonnet is for the sun, not for the length of the walk.

steps.explain: The lunch is the clue.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Look for something the children take that you would only need for a long time away.

questions.stem:
Read this short sentence. Which word best gives the meaning of ANALYSIS?

I am the presenter of a current affairs program called ‘PM’. ‘PM’ provides an analysis of what is happening in Australia and the rest of the world.
questions.hint: Think about what a news program does with events: it studies them carefully to explain them. Which option means to look at something closely?

steps.explain: Use the sentence to work out what “an analysis of what is happening” is.
steps.work: The program looks at the news and studies what is happening, so that it can explain it. An analysis is a close study of something.

steps.explain: Test each option in the sentence.
steps.work:
talkback — callers ringing in; not a study of the news.

discussion — people talking, but not necessarily studying closely.

check — to make sure something is right, which is not the meaning here.

examination — a close, careful look at something. ✓

steps.explain: Analysis and examination both mean a careful study.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: An analysis is a close, careful study of something.

questions.stem: ENCYCLOPAEDIA is to FACTS as DICTIONARY is to ?
questions.hint: Say what an encyclopaedia is full of. Then say what a dictionary is full of, using the same sentence pattern.

steps.explain: Find the link in the first pair.
steps.work: An ENCYCLOPAEDIA is a book that is full of FACTS. (a book → what it contains)

steps.explain: Use the same link for DICTIONARY. What is a dictionary full of?
steps.work: A DICTIONARY is a book that is full of words and their meanings — that is, VOCABULARY.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
GRAMMAR and SYNTAX are the rules for putting words together in sentences. A dictionary lists words, it does not teach those rules.

LITERACY is the ability to read and write, not something a dictionary contains.

steps.explain: The pair that matches ENCYCLOPAEDIA : FACTS is DICTIONARY : VOCABULARY.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Work out what an encyclopaedia contains, then ask what a dictionary contains.

questions.stem: When the following letters are rearranged they will make a word that means WITHOUT A CHANCE. Which letters will make this word?
questions.hint: Think of a word that means “with no chance”. Then see which set of letters can be rearranged to spell it.

steps.explain: Think of words that mean “without a chance”.
steps.work: Without a chance means there is no hope: HOPELESS.

steps.explain: Check that the letters of HOPELESS can be made from one of the options.
steps.work:
HOPELESS = H, O, P, E, L, E, S, S (8 letters)

LESSHOPE = L, E, S, S, H, O, P, E (8 letters) — the same letters!

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following information.

BUSINESS: COLLECTING AND SELLING YABBIES

NAME: Luke
AGE: 13
HOW IT WORKS: With a friend, Mathew (13), Luke uses three top nets and about twenty lines in different dams. They go after school and during weekends. Their best catch was 189 yabbies in 35 minutes. Their worst catch was 12 in 3 hours. On average they make \(\$15.00\)–\(\$20.00\), charging about \(\$1.10\) for a dozen yabbies. Already they have two regular clients.
PROBLEMS: It’s only a summer business.
GOOD THINGS: ‘We have lots of fun,’ says Luke.

BUSINESS: SUNDAY COMMUNITY MARKET STALL

NAME: Natasha
AGE: 14
HOW IT WORKS: After having a big clean-up of her bedroom, Natasha decided to ‘recycle’ her old toys and books by selling them.

You book a place for a table. It costs \(\$7.00\) to have a table inside, under cover. It costs \(\$5.00\) to be outside with your own table.

‘I made about \(\$67.00\) after I paid my brother back for the toys he gave me to sell. This money was shared with a friend who helped me’, says Natasha.

Lots of kids sell craft, such as hand-painted T-shirts, at the community markets. You can’t sell chocolates or food because of the health laws.

PROBLEMS: Natasha explains, ‘If it rains, not many people come. I don’t like it when many people say, “That’s too dear”, and walk away. Of course you need more things to sell each week.’
GOOD THINGS: ‘It’s fun to do with a friend. It makes cleaning up worthwhile. The money can be used to buy material to make more things’, she adds.

Source: Hazel Edwards, Kids With Working Ideas, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

parts.stem: What is the main topic of these two passages?
options: how to sell yabbies or craft
the problems and good things about two businesses
parts.hint: The main topic is the big idea that BOTH passages share. Ask: who are the passages about, and what are they all doing?

steps.explain: Find what the two passages have in common.
steps.work:
Luke (13) collects and sells yabbies.

Natasha (14) sells her old toys and books at a market.

Both are young people who are earning money by running a small business.

steps.explain: Check each option.
steps.work:
B — this only covers yabbies and craft, and does not say how to sell them.

C — the passages are about two young people, not how a business works in general.

D — “problems” and “good things” are just two of the headings used in each passage. They are not the main topic.

A — “how young people earned money” covers both passages. ✓

steps.explain: The main topic is how young people earned money.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: The main topic is the big idea shared by both passages.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

HALLOWEEN

Halloween started some 2000 years ago as the Samhain Festival. For the Celts it was a festival of the dead when evil spirits were thought to come out in the night.

In Europe, Halloween was thought of as a religious holiday to scare away evil spirits. The Christian Church brought Halloween into its own ritual. It became a way of honouring those Christian martyrs who had died and was celebrated on All Saint’s Day. Later All Saint’s Day was moved by some religions from May to November 1.

Trick or treating is now a way for children to obtain sweets. This began from a tradition in Ireland when villagers would leave gifts for the spirits outside their homes so that they would not enter their house.

Another Halloween tradition is the lantern. The Jack-O-Lantern was thought to be a lost spirit that could not find a place to rest. It wandered between heaven and hell eternally.

Dressing up in costumes such as goblins, witches or ghosts came about so that people could celebrate All Saint’s Day without any trouble from the evil spirits. Today Halloween is celebrated as a special event for the amusement of children. It has spread to Australia from the USA.

Source: adapted from Daily Illini, Erin Anadkat, 30 October 1998

parts.stem: What is the main idea of the article?
parts.hint: The main idea covers the WHOLE article. Which option is big enough to include every paragraph?

steps.explain: List what each paragraph is about.
steps.work:
1: how Halloween started (the Samhain Festival)

2: Halloween and the Church (All Saint’s Day)

3: trick or treating

4: the Jack-O-Lantern

5: dressing up and Halloween today

steps.explain: Find the idea that covers all five paragraphs.
steps.work: Every paragraph is about Halloween and where its customs came from — the tradition of Halloween.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Trick or treating, the Jack-O-Lantern and All Saint’s Day are each only one part of the article.

steps.explain: The main idea is the tradition of Halloween.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The main idea must cover the whole article, not just one paragraph.

parts.stem: How did Halloween begin?
options: It began as a festival of the dead
It began as a religious holiday.
It began as a Christian ritual.
parts.hint: Find the first sentence of the article. It tells you how Halloween started, before the Church changed it.

steps.explain: Read the very first sentence.
steps.work: “Halloween started some 2000 years ago as the Samhain Festival. For the Celts it was a festival of the dead when evil spirits were thought to come out in the night.”

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B and C — it became a religious holiday and a Christian ritual later, when the Church brought it into its own ritual.

D — “a holiday” is too general and does not say what the festival was for.

steps.explain: Halloween began as a festival of the dead.
steps.work: The answer is A.

parts.stem: What does this article show about Halloween?
options: how it became a religious holiday
how it became a US tradition
how it became a modern event
parts.hint: Follow the article from the first paragraph to the last. Where does Halloween end up, and how is it celebrated today?

steps.explain: Follow the story of Halloween through the paragraphs.
steps.work: It began as an old festival of the dead → the Church made it part of All Saint’s Day → customs like trick or treating, lanterns and costumes grew up → today it is a special event for children.

steps.explain: Look at the last paragraph for where the story ends.
steps.work: “Today Halloween is celebrated as a special event for the amusement of children.”

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Becoming a religious holiday is only one step in the middle. “US tradition” is not the main point (it only says it spread to Australia from the USA). “A holiday” is too general.

steps.explain: The article shows how Halloween became a modern event.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Think about how the whole article changes from beginning to end.

parts.stem: How many modern customs of Halloween are mentioned in this report?
parts.hint: Find the customs that are still done today (“now”, “today”). Do not count the things that happened 2000 years ago.

steps.explain: Find the customs that are mentioned and are still done today.
steps.work:
1. Trick or treating — “is now a way for children to obtain sweets”

parts.stem: Which of these statements about All Saint’s Day is correct?
options: It is now celebrated by some churches as All Hallows Day.
It was always celebrated by some churches in November.
It is still celebrated by some churches as a festival of the dead.
It used to be celebrated by some churches in May.
parts.hint: Find the sentence about All Saint’s Day being moved. Which month was it in before?

steps.explain: Find the sentence in the passage.
steps.work: “Later All Saint’s Day was moved by some religions from May to November 1.”

steps.explain: So some churches used to celebrate it in May.
steps.work: It was in May first, and it was moved to November later.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — “All Hallows Day” is not mentioned.

B — it was not always in November. It was moved there later.

C — the festival of the dead was the Celts’ festival, not All Saint’s Day.

steps.explain: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Find the sentence about All Saint’s Day in the passage. It mentions two months.

questions.stem: Which word best gives the meaning of BACKBONE?
questions.hint: Break the word into BACK and BONE. What is the long bone that runs down your back?

steps.explain: Break the word into two parts.
steps.work: BACK + BONE: the bone of the back.

steps.explain: Name the long line of bones that runs down the middle of your back.
steps.work: The long bone that protects the nerves in your back is the SPINE.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: REAR means the back part of something, REVERSE means opposite or backwards, STRUCTURE means how something is built. None names the bone.

steps.explain: Backbone and spine mean the same thing.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Split the word into BACK and BONE to find its meaning.

questions.hint: Look at which way each arrow points: right, then up, then left. How much does it turn each time, and which way is it turning?

steps.work: I points right, II points up, III points left.

| Car | Sold |
|---|---|
| Camry | 42 031 |
| Commodore | 107 514 |
| Corolla | 25 079 |
| Excel | 44 016 |
| Falcon | 79 615 |
| Festiva | 20 170 |
| Lancer | 17 161 |
| Magna | 35 644 |
| Pulsar | 19 835 |
| Starlet | 16 283 |

Source: VFACTS

Which was the fifth highest selling car in Australia?
questions.hint: The cars are in ABC order, not number order. Put the sales numbers in order from the biggest to the smallest, then count along to the fifth one.

steps.explain: Read the question carefully: the fifth HIGHEST, so we must rank the cars from the biggest number to the smallest.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in the series?

2  3  5  8  13  21  ?
questions.hint: Work out how much is added each time: 1, 2, 3, 5, … Do these gaps look like the numbers in the series itself?

steps.explain: Find the gap between each pair of neighbouring numbers.
steps.work: \(2\rightarrow3\) is \(+1\), \(3\rightarrow5\) is \(+2\), \(5\rightarrow8\) is \(+3\), \(8\rightarrow13\) is \(+5\), \(13\rightarrow21\) is \(+8\).

questions.stem: It cost \(\$44\) for one adult and one child to visit an amusement park and \(\$58\) for one adult and two children. How much is the cost for one adult to visit the amusement park?
questions.hint: Compare the two prices. What is different about the two groups of people, and how much more does the second group cost?

steps.explain: Write the two facts so they can be compared. Both groups have one adult; the second group has one more child.
steps.work:
1 adult + 1 child \(=\$44\)

1 adult + 2 children \(=\$58\)

questions.stem: You have 71 square tiles for an area. Make these into the largest possible square area using as many of the tiles as you can. How many tiles would you have left over?
questions.hint: A square area uses a square number of tiles: 1, 4, 9, 16, … Find the biggest square number that is not more than 71.

steps.explain: A square made of tiles has the same number of tiles along each side, so it uses a square number of tiles. List the square numbers near 71.
81 is more than 71, so 9 by 9 is too big. The largest square we can make is 8 tiles by 8 tiles.
steps.work: \(8\times8=64\) tiles

questions.stem: Sixty-four stamps cost \(\$28.80\). Which calculation do you use to work out the cost of one stamp?
questions.hint: To find the cost of ONE item when you know the total cost, share the total equally between all the items. Which operation shares equally?

steps.explain: Decide what we know and what we want to find.
steps.work:
Known: total cost \(=\$28.80\) for 64 stamps.

Wanted: the cost of 1 stamp.

steps.explain: Sharing a total equally between 64 stamps is division.
steps.work: cost of 1 stamp \(=\) total cost \(\div\) number of stamps \(=\$28.80\div64\)

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(45\text{c}\times64\) already uses the price of one stamp (45c), which we are trying to find — it would give the total.

C: \(64\div\$28.80\) divides the number of stamps by money.

D: \(64\times\$28.80\) would be the cost of 64 stamps if each stamp cost \(\$28.80\).

steps.explain: Work it out to see why A shows up as an option.
steps.work: \(28.80\div64=0.45\), so one stamp costs \(45\text{c}\). The calculation to use is \(\$28.80\div64\), option B.

keyPoints.note: You want the price of ONE: divide the total cost by the number of items.

questions.stem: Each shelf can hold up to five packets. How many shelves will I need to store nineteen packets?
questions.hint: Share the packets out five at a time. How many full shelves can you make, and what happens to the packets that are left over?

steps.explain: Each shelf holds at most 5 packets, so divide the 19 packets into groups of 5.
steps.work:
\(19\div5=3\) remainder \(4\)

3 full shelves hold \(3\times5=15\) packets. 4 packets are left over.

steps.explain: The 4 left-over packets still have to be stored, so they need one more shelf.

keyPoints.note: Each shelf holds at most 5, so work out how many groups of 5 you need.
Remember the packets that are left over after the full shelves still need a shelf.

questions.stem: My father married when he was 31 years old. My mother was born in 1925. They were married in 1947. How do you calculate the difference in their ages?
questions.hint: First work out the year the father was born. Then find the difference between the two birth years.

steps.explain: Find the year the father was born. He was 31 when they married in 1947.

steps.explain: The mother was born in 1925. Put both birth years on the line.

steps.explain: The difference in their ages is the later birth year take away the earlier birth year.
Check the other options.
Only option C is a correct calculation that gives 9 years.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: married when he was 31 years old
keyPoints.note: Take 31 away from the year of the wedding to find the father’s birth year.
A difference is found by subtracting the smaller birth year from the larger one.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

These figures show how much a family will spend to raise a child to age 17 years.

| Category | Amount |
|---|---|
| Housing | \(\$78\,015\) |
| Food | \(\$42\,553\) |
| Transportation | \(\$35\,461\) |
| Child care/education | \(\$21\,276\) |
| Clothing | \(\$16\,548\) |
| Health care | \(\$16\,548\) |
| Other (entertainment, books) | \(\$26\,005\) |
| TOTAL | \(\$236\,406\) |

These amounts are shown in the chart below but one of the categories is drawn incorrectly.

questions.stem:
What is the largest number that you can make from these seven digits?

1  1  3  5  8  2  9
questions.hint: The biggest digit in the first place makes the biggest number. Compare the four options place by place, from the left.

steps.explain: All four options use the same seven digits. To find which is the largest, compare them from the left, one place at a time.
The first digit is 5 in every option, and the second is 1 in every option. Now look at the third digit.
steps.work:
A has 1, B has 9, C has 1, D has 9.

A and C are smaller, so they are out. B and D both have 9.

steps.explain: Compare B and D at the fourth digit.
steps.work:
B 5 1 9 1 8 3 2 → the fourth digit is 1

D 5 1 9 2 8 1 3 → the fourth digit is 2

2 is greater than 1, so D is larger than B.

steps.explain: The largest of the numbers on offer is 5 192 813.
steps.work:
Note: if you could use the digits in any order, the largest number would be 9 853 211. It is not one of the options, so choose the largest option on the list.

The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Compare the numbers from the left: the first place where they differ decides which is bigger.

questions.stem: At an exhibition there were 432 men, 368 women and 59 children. Then 68 men, 32 women and 9 children left. How do we calculate how many remained?
questions.hint: People who left must be taken away, not added. Work out the total at the start, the total who left, and then subtract.

steps.explain: Find the total number of people at the start.
Find the total number who left.
The people who remained are the ones at the start take away the ones who left.
Check the options: the calculation must use subtraction between the two totals, and the result must be 750.
steps.work:
A gives \(850\) and C gives \(650\) — wrong results.

D adds the people who left, which is wrong.

B: \((432+368+59)-(68+32+9)=750\) ✓

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: People who left are taken away from the number at the start.
Remained means how many are still there, so subtract.

questions.stem:
Look at this clock. It is afternoon.

How many hours has it been since midnight?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 198 180" width="30%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t1-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="198" height="180"/></svg>

questions.hint: First read the time on the clock. Then count the hours from midnight to midday, and from midday to that time.

steps.explain: Read the time. The short (hour) hand points to 5 and the long (minute) hand points to 12.
steps.work: The time is 5 o’clock.

steps.explain: It is afternoon, so it is 5 pm. Count the hours since midnight in two parts.
steps.work:
Midnight to midday: \(12\) hours

Midday to 5 pm: \(5\) hours

steps.explain: Add the two parts.
Check: 5 hours would be the time since midday, and 15 or 16 hours would be 3 pm or 4 pm.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: In the afternoon, add 12 hours to the clock time to count the hours since midnight.
Midnight is 12:00 at night. Count from there.

questions.stem:
The following notes were shared among five children:

Which calculation below shows how to share the money equally?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 660 297" width="60%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t2-q3.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="660" height="297"/></svg>

questions.hint: First find how much money there is altogether. Then think: how do you share an amount equally between 5 children — multiply or divide?

steps.explain: Add up all the notes to find the total amount of money.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$185 altogether</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="183.78378378378378" height="34" rx="4" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="101.89189189189189" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$100</text><rect x="193.78378378378378" y="30" width="91.89189189189189" height="34" rx="4" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="239.7297297297297" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$50</text><rect x="285.6756756756757" y="30" width="36.75675675675676" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="304.05405405405406" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$20</text><rect x="322.43243243243245" y="30" width="18.37837837837838" height="34" rx="4" fill="#ede9fe" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="331.6216216216216" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$10</text><rect x="340.81081081081084" y="30" width="9.18918918918919" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="345.4054054054054" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$5</text></svg>

steps.explain: Sharing equally between 5 children means dividing the total by 5.
steps.work: \(185\div5=37\), so each child gets \(\$37\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$185 shared into 5 equal parts</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="68.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="44.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$37</text><rect x="78.0" y="30" width="68.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="112.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$37</text><rect x="146.0" y="30" width="68.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="180.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$37</text><rect x="214.0" y="30" width="68.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="248.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$37</text><rect x="282.0" y="30" width="68.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="316.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$37</text></svg>

steps.explain: Write the calculation. The brackets are needed so that all the notes are added before dividing.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \((185)\times5=925\) — multiplying makes the amount bigger, it does not share it.

B: with no brackets only the last note \(5\) is divided by \(5\) (division is done first): \(100+50+20+10+1=181\).

D: \((100+50+20+10+5)\times5\) multiplies instead of dividing.

steps.explain: Only option C shows the total shared equally between five children.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Sharing equally means dividing.
Divide by 5, after finding the total of all the notes.

| At work | 0.17 |
| While travelling | 0.08 |

options: Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or at work.

Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or while travelling.
Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or at a coffee shop.

steps.explain: “Most people” means the biggest groups. Find the two biggest numbers.
steps.work: At home: 70 and At work: 17 are the two largest.

steps.explain: Add them to see how many people that is.
steps.work: \(70+17=87\) out of 100 — most of the coffee drinkers.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B: work + coffee shop \(=17+4=21\)

C: home + travelling \(=70+8=78\) (home is right, but travelling is not the 2nd biggest)

D: home + coffee shop \(=70+4=74\)

Only “home or at work” (87) is the two biggest groups. The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: where people had their first cup of coffee
keyPoints.note: Use the table: the statement that is correct is about the two biggest numbers.

parts.stem: Assume that the figures in the table are correct for all groups of coffee drinkers. Out of 50 coffee drinkers, about how many would say they had their first cup of coffee at a coffee shop?
parts.hint: The table says 0.04 of 100 drinkers use a coffee shop. 50 is half of 100, so how many of the 4 would there be?

steps.explain: Find the coffee shop share in the table.
steps.work: Coffee shop: \(0.04=4\) out of \(100\) drinkers.

questions.stem: Every day from Monday to Friday, Anthony works from 7.30 am until 4.30 pm (including breaks for morning and afternoon tea plus lunch). How many hours is he at work altogether, including breaks?
questions.hint: First find how many hours Anthony is at work in ONE day. Then work out how many days he works.

steps.explain: Find the length of one working day: from 7.30 am to 4.30 pm.
steps.work:
7.30 am to 12.30 pm is \(5\) hours.

12.30 pm to 4.30 pm is \(4\) hours.

\(5+4=9\) hours each day

steps.explain: Count the days: Monday to Friday is 5 days.
steps.work: \(9\) hours \(\times\) \(5\) days

questions.stem: Which calculation shows you how to find the number of hundreds in 39 000?
questions.hint: To find how many hundreds fit into a number, ask: how many groups of 100 can you make from it? Which operation finds the number of groups?

steps.explain: “How many hundreds in 39 000?” means how many groups of 100 make up 39 000. Finding the number of groups is division.
Work it out and check with multiplication.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(39\,000\times100=3\,900\,000\) — far too big.

C: one-tenth of \(39\,000\) is \(3\,900\), and \(3\,900\times100=390\,000\) — too big.

D: \(100\div39\,000\) is a tiny number, much less than 1.

steps.explain: There are 390 hundreds in 39 000, found by dividing by 100.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This is a “how many groups” question. Groups are found by dividing.

questions.stem: In which general direction would you travel if you went directly from Sydney to Singapore?
questions.hint: Picture a map with north at the top. Is Singapore above or below Sydney, and is it to the left or to the right?

steps.explain: Picture a map of the world. Sydney is in the south of the world (southern hemisphere). Singapore is close to the equator.
steps.work: Singapore is NORTH of Sydney. (It is closer to the equator, so it is higher up the map.)

steps.explain: Is Singapore to the left (west) or to the right (east) of Sydney?
steps.work: Singapore is on the left of Sydney on a map: WEST of Sydney (Singapore is about 104° east, Sydney is about 151° east).

steps.explain: Put the two directions together.
steps.work: north + west = north-west

keyPoints.note: A general direction can be a mix, like north-west, if the place is both north and west.

questions.stem: There are 53 pupils who have to be divided into groups. The teacher first tries to divide them into 8 equal groups but there are some pupils left over. How many pupils would be left after the 8 groups?
questions.hint: Divide 53 by 8. How many pupils go into each group, and how many are left over? Use your 8 times table.

steps.explain: Find the biggest number that 8 groups can be made of, without going over 53 pupils. Use the 8 times table.
steps.work: \(8\times6=48\)   \(8\times7=56\) — too many.

steps.explain: So each group has 6 pupils, and 48 pupils are in groups.
The pupils left over are the ones not in a group.
Check: 48 + 5 = 53 ✓. The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Make as many equal groups as you can, and count the ones that do not fit.
The pupils left over are the remainder.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in the series?

21  42  84  ?
questions.hint: Look at how the numbers change. Is something being added each time (the gaps are 21, 42, …), or are the numbers being multiplied?

steps.explain: The gaps are not the same (21, then 42), so look at multiplying.
